paragraphs: Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, son of Shimon the martyr, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder.

A) In the Mishnah: Berakhot 1:1, 2; 2:5; 4:3; 6:8. Peah 2:4, 6; 4:5; 6:6. Demai 3:1. Sheviit 1:5; 9:5. Terumot 8:8. Maaser Sheni 2:7; 5:9. Challah 4:7, 8. Orlah 1:4. Bikkurim 2:6. Shabbat 12:6; 16:8. Eruvin 4:1, 2; 6:2; 10:1, 10. Pesachim 1:5; 3:4; 7:2; 10:5. Shekalim 6:1. Sukkah 2:1, 5; 3:9. Beitzah 1:8; 2:6; 3:2. Rosh Hashanah 1:6; 2:8, 9; 4:9. Taanit 1:3; 2:10. Moed Katan 3:6. Yevamot 5:1; 13:7; 16:7. Ketubbot 1:6, 7, 8, 9; 8:1; 13:3, 4, 5. Sotah 2:1. Gittin 1:1, 5. Bava Metzia 5:8, 10. Bava Batra 9:1. Shevuot 6:3. Eduyot 3:9, 10; 7:7. Avodah Zarah 3:4. Zevachim 9:1. Keritot 3:7. Kelim 5:4; 8:9; 12:3, 6; 17:2; 28:4. Negaim 6:5; 7:4. Parah 9:3; 11:1. Yadayim 3:1; 4:4. Tohorot 9:1.

B) He was patriarch after the destruction, after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, also in Yavneh, as appears in Rosh Hashanah chapter 4. “After Rabban Gamliel to Yavneh”: Sanhedrin 32. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai saved him from the emperor at the destruction of the Temple (M.). Asarah Maamarot, treatise Chikkur Din, part 2, chapter 19, writes: when Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, was killed, his son Gamliel of Yavneh was young. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai took his place and requested from Titus “the dynasty of R.B.” [דר״ב], Gittin 56—that is, that the patriarchate should not cease from his house. Yad Yehudah, section 129, writes concerning the statement that Gamliel of Yavneh was young: “However, Sefer Yuchasin says that Rabban Gamliel the Elder died eighteen years before the destruction and his son Shimon held the patriarchate during those eighteen years. Accordingly, Gamliel of Yavneh was at least twenty-three or twenty-four years old when his father was killed, for at the end of Yevamot it says that Rabban Gamliel remembered that people had been killed …, and Rabban Gamliel the Elder permitted their wives to marry on the testimony of one witness. There is no doubt that Gamliel of Yavneh was five or ten years old if he recalled a teaching and an incident from his mouth.” (In the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Arba Mitot, Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok was no less than ten years old when he testified that he saw a priest’s daughter burned with bundles of vine branches, and they told him, “A minor’s testimony is not valid”; see Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok.) “I saw that Abarbanel, on Avot, writes that they appointed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai patriarch after Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the Elder because he was close to the government. Yuchasin writes that Gamliel was not yet fit for the patriarchate when his father died. Perhaps this is what he meant by saying that he was young: too young for the patriarchate. However, it seems more likely that Titus killed Shimon, son of Gamliel the Elder, out of hatred for the patriarchs of the house of David. The sages could not appoint Gamliel of Yavneh patriarch in his place because of the king’s anger. They therefore appointed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who was not of David’s seed, because he was close to the government. Because he was close to the government, he asked the emperor to remove his wrath from the house of David and leave them the crown of the patriarchate. The emperor consented. This is correct and acceptable.” End of the quotation from Sefer Yad Yehudah. See Chiddushei Aggadot, chapter Eglah Arufah: Gamliel of Yavneh was patriarch at the time of the destruction; see there. This is not so, as stated above. He saw his grandfather Rabban Gamliel the Elder and the Temple, as stated above at the end of Yevamot. In chapter Keitzad Tzolin, 74a, Rabbi Tzadok said: “An incident with Rabban Gamliel, who told his slave Tavi, ‘Go and roast the Passover offering for us on the grill.’” Rashi explains: Gamliel lived in the Second Temple period, as we say in Gittin; Rabbi Yehoshua was among Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s students who carried him out on a bed at the destruction, and he was a disputant of Gamliel of Yavneh. Gamliel was a disputant of Rabbi Eliezer the Great and his brother-in-law, since Rabbi Eliezer married Imma Shalom, his sister.

C) Turnus Rufus decreed death against him. A governor came and said, “The man with the nose is being sought,” and Rabban Gamliel hid. The governor told him that if he saved him, he should bring him to the world to come. Rabban Gamliel swore to him, and the governor killed himself; if one of them died, the decree was annulled. A heavenly voice came forth saying that the governor was destined for the world to come. At the end of Taanit, 29a, Rashi explains: “A man of stature”—that is, the great man of the generation—“and I say, because he beautifies the face; so I found in the Arukh.” I, however, did not find it in the Arukh. Rather, Rashi there says: “The man with the nose: just as the nose beautifies the face, he beautifies his generation; that is, the leader of his generation is being sought to be killed.” Chiddushei Aggadot writes that a person’s life depends on the nose, as stated in chapter Yom HaKippurim from the verse “He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life”; so too Rabban Gamliel …. He blinded the eye of his slave Tavi and joyfully said to Rabbi Yehoshua, who was head of the court in his court, “Tavi has gone free.” But he did not go free, since one who admits liability to a fine is exempt: chapter Merubbeh, 74, end of side b; Jerusalem Talmud, end of Shevuot chapter 5, and end of chapter Ellu Nearot. He accepted condolences for his slave Tavi, who was worthy: Berakhot 16b. In the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of chapter Hamotze Tefillin: Tavi, Rabban Gamliel’s slave, would put on tefillin, and the sages did not protest. Sefer G.N., letter gimel, writes: Rabban Gamliel was the soul of Shem and Eber, and his slave was Ham—“a slave of slaves shall he be to his brothers.” Ham, in reduced numerical reckoning, is Tavi (requires examination). They said in Midrash Rabbah: Ham had many slaves fit to be ordained, like Tavi. Yoma 87a: “Canaan has many sons ….”

D) Rabban Gamliel’s maidservant was baking loaves of terumah, and at the last one she found herself impure. Rabban Gamliel said, “They are all impure.” Rashbam explains that this is Rabban Gamliel the Elder …. However, the Elder is usually called “Rabban Gamliel the Elder,” with the qualifier; it appears that this is Gamliel of Yavneh, colleague of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: Tosafot, Niddah 6b. In Chullin 5b: “Rabban Gamliel and his court hold like Rabbi Meir.” Rashi explains that this implies Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, who was after Rabbi Meir. This is difficult, since everywhere he is usually called Gamliel Berabbi or Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi; rather, this is Gamliel of Yavneh (Tosafot). In Tosafot, beginning of chapter Hadar: it should have specified explicitly “Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi”; one must therefore say that this is Gamliel of Yavneh. The reason it says that Gamliel and his court hold like Rabbi Meir is that Rabbi Meir holds this explicitly. Sefer Maginnei Shelomoh answers Tosafot’s difficulty: bar Kappara, the author of the teaching, lived in the days of Gamliel Berabbi, for bar Kappara lived in Rabbi’s days (see his entry). One may therefore say that Gamliel was still alive when he stated this teaching, so he said to his students simply “Rabban Gamliel,” and they knew that he meant him (see above, Rabbi Yehudah Nesia). Although at the beginning of chapter Mi Shemet Shmuel said, “This is the opinion of Gamliel Berabbi,” even though Shmuel lived in Rabbi’s days and Gamliel ruled after Rabbi; and likewise Rabbi Yochanan, in chapter Kol HaBasar, said, “I asked Gamliel Berabbi”—one may say that they nevertheless stated those teachings after his death, and had to say “Gamliel Berabbi” so that we should not err, since he had already died. In Yevamot 15a: an incident with Gamliel’s daughter, who was married to his brother Abba, who died without sons. Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her co-wife; his daughter was an aylonit. Rashi explains that Gamliel was among Hillel’s descendants. This must be Gamliel of Yavneh: first, it is not usual to call Rabban Gamliel the Elder simply Gamliel, as above; second, the Elder was Hillel’s grandson, whereas Rashi’s wording “among his descendants” proves that this is Gamliel of Yavneh. He is called Berabbi in Shabbat, chapter Kol Kitvei, 115a, and chapter Shoel, 151b. Rabbi Yose said: “An incident with Abba Chalafta, who went to Gamliel Berabbi”—in Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 14, the word Berabbi is absent—“in Tiberias and found him sitting at Yochanan HaNazuf’s table”—there: Ben Nazuf—“with a book of Job in translation in his hand, reading it. He said to him, ‘I remember your grandfather, Rabban Gamliel the Elder, standing on a step on the Temple Mount. They brought him a book of Job in translation, and he told the builder, “Sink it into the building.”’” Rashi explains: “Gamliel Berabbi does not mean that he was Rabbi’s son, but that he was a great man of his generation; this Gamliel was our holy master’s grandfather.” End of Rashi’s words. In Kiddushin 32b: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Tzadok were reclining at the feast for Gamliel’s son, and Gamliel was standing and serving them drink. He gave the cup to Rabbi Eliezer, who did not take it; he gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua, who took it. Rabbi Eliezer said to him, “We are sitting, while Gamliel Berabbi stands and serves us drink.” (In newer Talmud editions Berabbi was deleted, not because he was not called Berabbi—for afterwards Rabbi Yehoshua called him Berabbi, and Rashi explained, “That is, a great man”—but because Rashi comments on Rabbi Yehoshua’s words, “Let Gamliel Berabbi not …,” proving that Rabbi Eliezer did not call him Berabbi. But the reading in Ein Yaakov, also in Rabbi Eliezer’s words, is “while Gamliel Berabbi stands”; so too in Sifrei, beginning of section Ekev.) Rabbi Yehoshua said to him, “We find that our father Abraham was the great man of his generation, yet he stood over them; and as for us, should Gamliel Berabbi not stand …?” In Niddah 63b: Gamliel Berabbi in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel—he is the father of Shimon the martyr, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder. See above, Berabbi and Rabbi Tarfon, concerning Gamliel’s being called Berabbi. In chapter Mi Shemet, 139b: “This is the opinion of Gamliel Berabbi.” Maharit, Ketubbot 108, writes that this is Gamliel of Yavneh. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said, “How many times Akiva ben Yosef was punished because I complained about him before Gamliel Berabbi!”

E) In Sanhedrin 11b: “Come and see the difference between the stern men of old”—Rabban Gamliel, who exercised authority and instilled fear in the students, as we find in Bekhorot, Berakhot, and Rosh Hashanah, where he distressed Rabbi Yehoshua; nevertheless he wrote “The matter seems good before me and before my colleagues”; Rashi—“an incident in which Gamliel was sitting on a step on the Temple Mount, Yochanan the scribe stood before him, and three letters were before him. He said, ‘Write to our brothers of Upper and Lower Galilee …,’ to the people of the south and to the exiles in Babylonia, ‘And the matter seems good …’”—“and the humble men of later times”—as we say in chapter Hasokher et HaPoalim, yet he did not say “before my colleagues”; Rashi. It objects: “Perhaps this was after they removed him”—meaning that he had a colleague, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who was patriarch with him, and therefore said “before my colleagues”; Tosafot. See the Jerusalem Talmud, end of the last chapter of Maaser Sheni. The incident in which Gamliel accepted testimony about the new moon: Rabbi Dosa ben Horkenos said, “They are false witnesses,” and Rabbi Yehoshua agreed with him. Gamliel decreed that Rabbi Yehoshua should come with his staff and money on the Day of Atonement according to his calculation. He came to him on the Day of Atonement; Gamliel kissed Rabbi Yehoshua on his head and said, “Come in peace, my teacher and my student”: Rosh Hashanah 25a. Proklos ben Pelosofos questioned him in Akko: Avodah Zarah 44b. A philosopher questioned him: 54b. He cherished the commandments, buying an etrog for one thousand zuz: Sukkah 41b. Rabbi Akiva said, “I asked Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, who had gone to buy an animal for the feast for Gamliel’s son at the meat market of Immaum”: Keritot 15a–b. Tosafot Chadashim writes there: this tells their praise, for although they were occupied, they engaged in words of Torah. Because of the dispute he had with Rabbi Yehoshua, although he loved him and gave him the tithes, they gave the patriarchate to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah (see his entry). From his great piety and desire for Torah, he did not keep himself from the study house. They restored the patriarchate to him; he expounded for two Sabbaths and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah for one Sabbath (see his entry). Gilgulei Neshamot, letter alef, writes: “Gamliel was a reincarnation of Nechemyah. Because Nechemyah said, ‘Remember me, my God, for good,’ Gamliel was driven from his patriarchate, just as the book of Nechemyah was not called by his name.” End of quotation. Gamliel was riding a donkey on the road from Akko to Keziv, and Rabbi Ilai walked behind him. He found a loaf on the road and said, “Ilai, take this loaf and give it to Mavgai.” Although he did not know him, he discerned through the holy spirit that his name was Mavgai: Eruvin 64b; Jerusalem Talmud, Avodah Zarah chapter 1, halakhah 9; Midrash Rabbah, end of section Bechukkotai. Gamliel and the elders were reclining in an upper room in Jericho. Gamliel gave Rabbi Akiva permission to recite the blessing …. Gamliel said to him, “Akiva, how long will you put your head into a dispute?” He answered, “Our master …; thus you taught us, our master”: Berakhot 37a. Through the falling on his face of Rabbi Eliezer the Great, his brother-in-law, because they had ‘blessed’ him, Gamliel died (see his entry). At his death Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were present (see above, Rabban Gamliel the Elder). Rabbi Yehoshua wanted to annul all the rulings that had been against him, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, his colleague and Rabbi Yehoshua’s colleague, stood against him and did not let him, as stated in Eruvin 41a. (Sefer Nachalat Shimoni writes, “After Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s death, Rabbi Yehoshua wanted …”; he erred.) Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said, “I see that the body follows the head; all the time that Gamliel was alive …” (Tosefta Taanit, chapter 2). With Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, the law follows Gamliel (M.K.). G.A.Y. writes: Rabban Gamliel is buried in a large domed structure in Yavneh. Berakhot 16b: he bathed on the first night after his wife died, saying that he was delicate. For it is found among the kabbalists that six souls were implanted in Gamliel: the soul of Abraham, who had an element of the husk on account of his son Ishmael; the soul of Rav Sechora; Rav Tavyomi; Nachum of Elkosh; Yehudah ben Yaakov; and Rabbi Simon—bar Abba, as written at the end of Sefer G.N.; no Rabbi Simon bar Abba is found throughout the Talmud. Gamliel therefore always bathed to repair and atone for these souls. The kabbalist, our teacher Rabbi Sh. Maggid, said of this: “This is the secret of istenis: the initials of Abraham, Sechora, Tavyomi, Nachum, Yehudah, Simon.” End of quotation. But this is very puzzling to me: Gamliel of Yavneh preceded Rav Tavyomi, who is Mar son of Rav Ashi, Rav Sechora, and Rav Simon by many generations; examine it and you will find this. Since Gamliel preceded them by so much, how could he have been implanted with their souls? One cannot say that these six souls were in Gamliel and afterwards came into the three aforementioned righteous men, Tavyomi, Sechora, and Simon, for it writes that they came to repair those souls in him. This requires examination.

F) Abba Guryon in his name; Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok in his name. Chizkiyah, father of Ikkesh, testified before him. Rabbi Chanina was his son. See Chananya, son of Rabbi Yehoshua’s brother. Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya and Rabbi Yehudah, son of Rabbi Ilai, studied before him. Rabbi Yonatan ben Charsha of Ginosar questioned him in Yavneh. Rabbi Yose ben Taddai of Tiberias questioned Gamliel. Rabbi Yose in his name; Rabbi Yose, son of Rabbi Elazar, in his name. Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi’s father, was his son. Rabbi Shimon ben Guda and Rabbi Shimon ben Goda testified about him before his son.
